The force magnitudes are $F_1 = 5.00\text{ N}$, $F_2 = 9.00\text{ N}$, and $F_3 = 3.00\text{ N}$, and the indicated angle is $\theta = 60.0^\circ$. A military helicopter lifts a $75\text{ kg}$ flood survivor $16\text{ m}$ vertically from the river by a rope. If the acceleration of the survivor is $g/10$, how much work is done on the survivor by (a) the force from the helicopter and (b) the gravitational force on her? Just before she reaches the helicopter, what are her (c) kinetic energy and (d) speed?

In Fig. 7-23, a block of ice slides down a frictionless ramp at angle $50^\circ$ while an ice worker pulls on the block (via a rope) with a force that has a magnitude of $50\text{ N}$ and is directed up the ramp. As the block slides through distance $d = 0.50\text{ m}$ along the ramp, its kinetic energy increases by $80\text{ J}$. How much greater would its kinetic energy have been if the rope had not been attached to the block?

A cord is used to vertically lower an initially stationary block of mass $M$ at a constant downward acceleration of $g/4$. When the block has fallen a distance $d$, find (a) the work done by the cord’s force on the block, (b) the work done by the gravitational force on the block, (c) the kinetic energy of the block, and (d) the speed of the block.

In Fig. 7-25, a constant force $\vec{F}_a$ of magnitude $82.0\text{ N}$ is applied to a $3.00\text{ kg}$ shoe box at angle $\phi = 53.0^\circ$, causing the box to move up a frictionless ramp at constant speed. How much work is done on the box by $\vec{F}_a$ when the box has moved through vertical distance $h = 0.150\text{ m}$?

In Fig. 7-27, a $0.250\text{ kg}$ block of cheese lies on the floor of a $900\text{ kg}$ elevator cab that is being pulled upward by a cable through distance $d_1 = 2.40\text{ m}$ and then through distance $d_2 = 10.5\text{ m}$. (a) Through $d_1$, if the normal force on the block from the floor has constant magnitude $F_N = 3.00\text{ N}$, how much work is done on the cab by the force from the cable? (b) Through $d_2$, if the work done on the cab by the (constant) force from the cable is $92.61\text{ kJ}$, what is the magnitude of $F_N$?

A spring and block are in the arrangement of Fig. 7-10. When the block is pulled out to $x = +4.0\text{ cm}$, we must apply a force of magnitude $360\text{ N}$ to hold it there. We pull the block to $x = 11\text{ cm}$ and then release it. How much work does the spring do on the block as the block moves from $x_i = +5.0\text{ cm}$ to (a) $x = +3.0\text{ cm}$, (b) $x = -3.0\text{ cm}$, (c) $x = -5.0\text{ cm}$, and (d) $x = -9.0\text{ cm}$?

In the arrangement of Fig. 7-10, we gradually pull the block from $x = 0$ to $x = +3.0\text{ cm}$, where it is stationary. Figure 7-28 gives the work that our force does on the block. The scale of the figure’s vertical axis is set by $W_s = 1.0\text{ J}$. We then pull the block out to $x = +5.0\text{ cm}$ and release it from rest. How much work does the spring do on the block when the block moves from $x_i = +5.0\text{ cm}$ to (a) $x = +4.0\text{ cm}$, (b) $x = -2.0\text{ cm}$, and (c) $x = -5.0\text{ cm}$?

As a $2.5\text{ kg}$ body moves in the positive direction along an $x$ axis, a single force acts on it. The force is given by $F_x = -6x\text{ N}$, with $x$ in meters. The velocity at $x = 3.5\text{ m}$ is $8.5\text{ m/s}$. (a) Find the velocity of the body at $x = 4.5\text{ m}$. (b) Find the positive value of $x$ at which the body has a velocity of $5.5\text{ m/s}$.

The block in Fig. 7-10a lies on a horizontal frictionless surface, and the spring constant is $50\text{ N/m}$. Initially, the spring is at its relaxed length and the block is stationary at position $x = 0$. Then an applied force with a constant magnitude of $3.0\text{ N}$ pulls the block in the positive direction of the $x$ axis, stretching the spring until the block stops. When that stopping point is reached, what are (a) the position of the block, (b) the work that has been done on the block by the applied force, and (c) the work that has been done on the block by the spring force? During the block’s displacement, what are (d) the block’s position when its kinetic energy is maximum and (e) the value of that maximum kinetic energy?

The force on a particle is directed along an $x$ axis and given by $F = F_0(x/x_0 - 1)$. Find the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x = 0$ to $x = 2x_0$ by (a) plotting $F(x)$ and measuring the work from the graph and (b) integrating $F(x)$.

Figure 7-33 gives the acceleration of a $2.00\text{ kg}$ particle as an applied force moves it from rest along an $x$ axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 9.0\text{ m}$. The scale of the figure’s vertical axis is set by $a_s = 6.0\text{ m/s}^2$. How much work has the force done on the particle when the particle reaches (a) $x = 4.0\text{ m}$, (b) $x = 7.0\text{ m}$, and (c) $x = 9.0\text{ m}$? What is the particle’s speed and direction of travel when it reaches (d) $x = 4.0\text{ m}$, (e) $x = 7.0\text{ m}$, and (f) $x = 9.0\text{ m}$?
options: (a) $42\text{ J}$; (b) $30\text{ J}$; (c) $12\text{ J}$; (d) $6.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $5.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $3.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $50\text{ J}$; (b) $35\text{ J}$; (c) $18\text{ J}$; (d) $7.1\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $6.0\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $4.2\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $36\text{ J}$; (b) $24\text{ J}$; (c) $8\text{ J}$; (d) $5.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $4.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $2.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $42\text{ J}$; (b) $30\text{ J}$; (c) $12\text{ J}$; (d) $6.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis; (e) $5.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis; (f) $3.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis

q: A particle of mass $0.020\text{ kg}$ moves along a curve with velocity $\vec{v}_1 = (5.0\hat{i} + 18\hat{k})\text{ m/s}$. After some time, the velocity changes to $\vec{v}_2 = (9.0\hat{i} + 22\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ due to the action of a single force. Find the work done on the particle during this interval of time.

Only one force is acting on a $2.8\text{ kg}$ particle-like object whose position is given by $x = 4.0t - 5.0t^2 + 2.0t^3$, with $x$ in meters and $t$ in seconds. What is the work done by the force from $t = 0\text{ s}$ to $t = 6.0\text{ s}$?

A force of $5.0\text{ N}$ acts on a $15\text{ kg}$ body initially at rest. Compute the work done by the force in (a) the first, (b) the second, and (c) the third seconds and (d) the instantaneous power due to the force at the end of the third second.

Across a horizontal floor, a $102\text{ kg}$ block is pulled at a constant speed of $5.5\text{ m/s}$ by an applied force of $125\text{ N}$ directed $38^\circ$ above the horizontal. Calculate the rate at which the force does work on the block.

A machine carries a $4.0\text{ kg}$ package from an initial position of $\vec{d}_i = (0.50\hat{i} + 0.75\hat{j} + 0.20\hat{k})\text{ m}$ at $t = 0$ to a final position of $\vec{d}_f = (7.50\hat{i} + 12.0\hat{j} + 7.20\hat{k})\text{ m}$ at $t = 12\text{ s}$. The constant force applied by the machine on the package is $\vec{F} = (2.00\hat{i} + 4.00\hat{j} + 6.00\hat{k})\text{ N}$. For that displacement, find (a) the work done on the package by the machine’s force and (b) the average power of the machine’s force on the package.

A fully loaded, slow-moving freight elevator has a cab with a total mass of $1200\text{ kg}$, which is required to travel upward $54\text{ m}$ in $3.0\text{ min}$, starting and ending at rest. The elevator’s counterweight has a mass of only $950\text{ kg}$, and so the elevator motor must help. What average power is required of the force the motor exerts on the cab via the cable?

A force $\vec{F} = (3.00\hat{i} + 7.00\hat{j} + 7.00\hat{k})\text{ N}$ acts on a $2.00\text{ kg}$ mobile object that moves from an initial position of $\vec{d}_i = (3.00\hat{i} - 2.00\hat{j} + 5.00\hat{k})\text{ m}$ to a final position of $\vec{d}_f = (-5.00\hat{i} + 4.00\hat{j} + 7.00\hat{k})\text{ m}$ in $4.00\text{ s}$. Find (a) the work done on the object by the force in the $4.00\text{ s}$ interval, (b) the average power due to the force during that interval, and (c) the angle between vectors $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{d}_f - \vec{d}_i$.

Adam stretches a spring by some length. John stretches the same spring later by three times the length stretched by Adam. Find the ratio of the stored energy in the first stretch to that in the second stretch.

You drop a $2.00\text{ kg}$ book to a friend who stands on the ground at distance $D = 10.0\text{ m}$ below. Your friend’s outstretched hands are at distance $d = 1.50\text{ m}$ above the ground (Fig. 8-19). (a) How much work $W_g$ does the gravitational force do on the book as it drops to her hands? (b) What is the change $\Delta U$ in the gravitational potential energy of the book–Earth system during the drop? If the gravitational potential energy $U$ of that system is taken to be zero at ground level, what is $U$ (c) when the book is released, and (d) when it reaches her hands? Now take $U$ to be $100\text{ J}$ at ground level and again find (e) $W_g$, (f) $\Delta U$, (g) $U$ at the release point, and (h) $U$ at her hands.

In Fig. 8-21, a $2.00\text{ g}$ ice flake is released from the edge of a hemispherical bowl whose radius $r$ is $22.0\text{ cm}$. The flake–bowl contact is frictionless. (a) How much work is done on the flake by the gravitational force during the flake’s descent to the bottom of the bowl? (b) What is the change in the potential energy of the flake–Earth system during that descent? (c) If that potential energy is taken to be zero at the bottom of the bowl, what is its value when the flake is released? (d) If, instead, the potential energy is taken to be zero at the release point, what is its value when the flake reaches the bottom of the bowl? (e) If the mass of the flake were doubled, would the magnitudes of the answers to (a) through (d) increase, decrease, or remain the same?
options: (a) $4.31\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-4.31\text{ mJ}$; (c) $4.31\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-4.31\text{ mJ}$; (e) all increase
(a) $2.15\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-2.15\text{ mJ}$; (c) $2.15\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-2.15\text{ mJ}$; (e) all decrease
(a) $8.62\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-8.62\text{ mJ}$; (c) $8.62\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-8.62\text{ mJ}$; (e) remain the same

q: Figure 8-23 shows a thin rod, of length $L = 2.00\text{ m}$ and negligible mass, that can pivot about one end to rotate in a vertical circle. A ball of mass $m = 5.00\text{ kg}$ is attached to the other end. The rod is pulled aside to angle $\theta_0 = 30.0^\circ$ and released with initial velocity $\vec{v}_0 = 0$. As the ball descends to its lowest point, (a) how much work does the gravitational force do on it and (b) what is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the ball–Earth system? (c) If the gravitational potential energy is taken to be zero at the lowest point, what is its value just as the ball is released? (d) Do the magnitudes of the answers to (a) through (c) increase, decrease, or remain the same if angle $\theta_0$ is increased?
options: (a) $9.8\text{ J}$; (b) $-9.8\text{ J}$; (c) $9.8\text{ J}$; (d) remain the same

q: In Problem 2, what is the speed of the car at (a) point A, (b) point B, and (c) point C? (d) How high will the car go on the last hill, which is too high for it to cross? (e) If we substituted a second car with twice the mass, what then are the answers to parts (a) through (d)?
options: (a) $17.0\text{ m/s}$; (b) $26.5\text{ m/s}$; (c) $33.4\text{ m/s}$; (d) $56.7\text{ m}$; (e) all the same
(a) $12.0\text{ m/s}$; (b) $20.0\text{ m/s}$; (c) $28.0\text{ m/s}$; (d) $40.0\text{ m}$; (e) all double
(a) $17.0\text{ m/s}$; (b) $26.5\text{ m/s}$; (c) $33.4\text{ m/s}$; (d) $56.7\text{ m}$; (e) all double

q: (a) In Problem 5, what is the speed of the flake when it reaches the bottom of the bowl? (b) If we substituted a second flake with twice the mass, what would its speed be? (c) If, instead, we gave the flake an initial downward speed along the bowl, would the answer to part (a) increase, decrease, or remain the same?

A $5.0\text{ g}$ marble is fired vertically upward using a spring gun. The spring must be compressed $8.0\text{ cm}$ if the marble is to just reach a target $20\text{ m}$ above the marble’s position on the compressed spring. (a) What is the change $\Delta U_g$ in the gravitational potential energy of the marble–Earth system during the $20\text{ m}$ ascent? (b) What is the change $\Delta U_s$ in the elastic potential energy of the spring during its launch of the marble? (c) What is the spring constant of the spring?

In Fig. 8-24, a runaway truck with failed brakes is moving downgrade at $130\text{ km/h}$ just before the driver steers the truck up a frictionless emergency escape ramp with an inclination of $\theta = 15^\circ$. The truck’s mass is $1.2 \times 10^4\text{ kg}$. (a) What minimum length $L$ must the ramp have if the truck is to stop (momentarily) along it? (b) Does the minimum length $L$ increase, decrease, or remain the same if the truck’s mass is decreased and (c) its speed is decreased?

In Problem 6, what are the magnitudes of (a) the horizontal component and (b) the vertical component of the net force acting on the block at point Q? (c) At what height $h$ should the block be released from rest so that it is on the verge of losing contact with the track at the top of the loop? (d) Graph the magnitude of the normal force on the block at the top of the loop versus initial height $h$, for the range $h = 0$ to $h = 6R$.

A $1.0\text{ kg}$ block moving at $8.0\text{ m/s}$ strikes a spring fixed at one end to a wall and compresses the spring by $0.40\text{ m}$, where its speed gets reduced to $2.0\text{ m/s}$. After this event, the spring is mounted upright by fixing its bottom end to a floor, and a stone of mass $2.0\text{ kg}$ is placed on it; the spring is now compressed by $0.50\text{ m}$ from its rest length. The system is then released. How far above the rest-length point does the stone rise?

Figure 8-23 shows a pendulum of length $L = 1.25\text{ m}$. Its bob (which effectively has all the mass) has speed $v_0$ when the cord makes an angle $\theta_0 = 40.0^\circ$ with the vertical. (a) What is the speed of the bob when it is in its lowest position if $v_0 = 8.00\text{ m/s}$? What is the least value that $v_0$ can have if the pendulum is to swing down and then up (b) to a horizontal position, and (c) to a vertical position with the cord remaining straight? (d) Do the answers to parts (b) and (c) increase, decrease, or remain the same if $\theta_0$ is increased by a few degrees?
options: (a) $9.50\text{ m/s}$; (b) $5.50\text{ m/s}$; (c) $8.80\text{ m/s}$; (d) remain the same

q: The string in Fig. 8-26 is $L = 120\text{ cm}$ long, has a ball attached to one end, and is fixed at its other end. The distance $d$ from the fixed end to a fixed peg at point P is $75.0\text{ cm}$. When the initially stationary ball is released with the string horizontal as shown, it will swing along the dashed arc. What is its speed when it reaches (a) its lowest point and (b) its highest point after the string catches on the peg?

At $t = 0$ a $1.0\text{ kg}$ ball is thrown from a tall tower with $\vec{v}_0 = (18\text{ m/s})\hat{i} + (24\text{ m/s})\hat{j}$. What is $\Delta U$ of the ball–Earth system between $t = 0$ and $t = 6.0\text{ s}$ (still free fall)?

Tarzan, who weighs $688\text{ N}$, swings from a cliff at the end of a vine $18\text{ m}$ long (Fig. 8-28). From the top of the cliff to the bottom of the swing, he descends by $3.2\text{ m}$. The vine will break if the force on it exceeds $950\text{ N}$. (a) Does the vine break? (b) If it does not, what is the greatest force on it during the swing? If it does, at what angle with the vertical does it break?

A $4.00\text{ kg}$ block moves on a horizontal, frictionless surface and collides with a spring of spring constant $k$ that is fixed to a wall. When the block momentarily stops, the spring has been compressed by $0.20\text{ m}$. After rebounding, the block has a speed of $4.00\text{ m/s}$. Next, the spring is put on an inclined surface with its lower end fixed in place (Fig. 8-30). The same block is now released on the incline at a distance of $5.00\text{ m}$ from the spring’s free end. When the block momentarily stops, the spring has been compressed by $0.30\text{ m}$. (a) What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline? (b) How far does the block then move up the incline from the stopping point?

As shown in Fig. 8-32, the right end of a spring is fixed to a wall. A $1.00\text{ kg}$ block is then pushed against the free end so that the spring is compressed by $0.25\text{ m}$. After the block is released, it slides along a horizontal floor and (after leaving the spring) up an incline; both floor and incline are frictionless. Its maximum (vertical) height on the incline is $5.00\text{ m}$. What are (a) the spring constant and (b) the maximum speed? (c) If the angle of the incline is increased, what happens to the maximum (vertical) height?

In Fig. 8-34, a spring with $k = 170\text{ N/m}$ is at the top of a frictionless incline of angle $37.0^\circ$. The lower end of the incline is distance $D = 1.00\text{ m}$ from the end of the spring, which is at its relaxed length. A $2.00\text{ kg}$ canister is pushed against the spring until the spring is compressed $0.200\text{ m}$ and released from rest. (a) What is the speed of the canister at the instant the spring returns to its relaxed length (which is when the canister loses contact with the spring)? (b) What is the speed of the canister when it reaches the lower end of the incline?

In Fig. 8-30, a block of mass $m = 3.20\text{ kg}$ slides from rest a distance $d$ down a frictionless incline at angle $\theta = 30.0^\circ$ where it runs into a spring of spring constant $431\text{ N/m}$. When the block momentarily stops, it has compressed the spring by $21.0\text{ cm}$. What are (a) distance $d$ and (b) the distance between the point of the first block–spring contact and the point where the block’s speed is greatest?

At a lunar base, a uniform chain hangs over the edge of a horizontal platform. A machine does $1.0\text{ J}$ of work in pulling the rest of the chain onto the platform. The chain has a mass of $2.0\text{ kg}$ and a length of $3.0\text{ m}$. What length was initially hanging over the edge? On the Moon, the gravitational acceleration is $1/6$ of $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

Figure 8-38 shows a plot of potential energy $U$ versus position $x$ of a $0.90\text{ kg}$ particle that can travel only along an $x$ axis. Three values are $U_A = 15.0\text{ J}$, $U_B = 35.0\text{ J}$, and $U_C = 45.0\text{ J}$. The particle is released at $x = 4.5\text{ m}$ with an initial speed of $7.0\text{ m/s}$, headed in the negative $x$ direction. (a) If the particle can reach $x = 1.0\text{ m}$, what is its speed there, and if it cannot, what is its turning point? What are the (b) magnitude and (c) direction of the force on the particle as it begins to move to the left of $x = 4.0\text{ m}$?
options: (a) $2.1\text{ m/s}$; (b) $10\text{ N}$; (c) $+x$ direction; (d) $5.7\text{ m}$; (e) $30\text{ N}$; (f) $-x$ direction
(a) $3.5\text{ m/s}$; (b) $15\text{ N}$; (c) $-x$ direction; (d) $4.2\text{ m}$; (e) $20\text{ N}$; (f) $+x$ direction

q: A single conservative force $F(x)$ acts on a $1.0\text{ kg}$ particle that moves along an $x$ axis. The potential energy $U(x)$ associated with $F(x)$ is given by $U(x) = -4x e^{-x/4}\text{ J}$, where $x$ is in meters. At $x = 5.0\text{ m}$ the particle has a kinetic energy of $2.0\text{ J}$. (a) What is the mechanical energy of the system?

In Fig. 8-39, a $3.5\text{ kg}$ block is accelerated from rest by a compressed spring of spring constant $640\text{ N/m}$. The block leaves the spring at the spring’s relaxed length and then travels over a horizontal floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.25$. The frictional force stops the block in distance $D = 7.8\text{ m}$. What are (a) the increase in the thermal energy of the block–floor system, (b) the maximum kinetic energy of the block, and (c) the original compression distance of the spring?

A loaded truck of mass $3000\text{ kg}$ moves on a level road at a constant speed of $6.000\text{ m/s}$. The frictional force on the truck from the road is $1000\text{ N}$. Assume that air drag is negligible. (a) How much work is done by the truck engine in $10.00\text{ min}$? (b) After $10.00\text{ min}$, the truck enters a hilly region whose inclination is $30^\circ$ and continues to move with the same speed for another $10.00\text{ min}$. What is the total work done by the engine during that period against the gravitational force and the frictional force? (c) What is the total work done by the engine in the full $20\text{ min}$?

A small block of mass $1/4\text{ kg}$ has an initial kinetic energy of $500\text{ J}$ while moving over the frictionless surface shown in Fig. 8-40. (a) Find the kinetic energy of block at Q. (b) If we assume that the potential energy at P is equal to zero, what is the potential energy of the block at R? (c) Find the speed of the block at R. (d) Find the change in the potential energy as the block moves from Q to R.

In Fig. 8-42, a $50\text{ kg}$ child rides a $2.0\text{ kg}$ seat down a frictionless slope from a height of $7.0\text{ m}$. Upon reaching the floor, the child and seat slide along it. There the coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.30$. How far along the floor do they slide?

In Fig. 8-43, a block of mass $m$ slides down three slides, each from a height $H$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is the same value $\mu$ for the slides. In terms of $m, H, \mu$, and $g$, what is the final kinetic energy of the block as it emerges from (a) slide a, (b) slide b, and (c) slide c?
A swimmer moves through the water at an average speed of $0.22\text{ m/s}$. The average drag force is $110\text{ N}$. What average power is required of the swimmer?

The total mechanical energy of a $2.00\text{ kg}$ particle moving along an $x$ axis is $5.00\text{ J}$. The potential energy is given as $U(x) = (x^4 - 2.00x^2)\text{ J}$, with $x$ in meters. Find the maximum velocity.

A block of mass $6.0\text{ kg}$ is pushed up an incline to its top by a man and then allowed to slide down to the bottom. The length of incline is $10\text{ m}$ and its height is $5.0\text{ m}$. The coefficient of friction between block and incline is $0.40$. Calculate (a) the work done by the gravitational force over the complete round trip of the block, (b) the work done by the man during the upward journey, (c) the mechanical energy loss due to friction over the round trip, and (d) the speed of the block when it reaches the bottom.

A stone with a weight of $5.29\text{ N}$ is launched vertically from ground level with an initial speed of $20.0\text{ m/s}$, and the air drag on it is $0.265\text{ N}$ throughout the flight. What are (a) the maximum height reached by the stone and (b) its speed just before it hits the ground?

A $10.0\text{ kg}$ block falls $30.0\text{ m}$ onto a vertical spring whose lower end is fixed to a platform. When the spring reaches its maximum compression of $0.200\text{ m}$, it is locked in place. The block is then removed and the spring apparatus is transported to the Moon, where the gravitational acceleration is $g/6$. A $50.0\text{ kg}$ astronaut then sits on top of the spring and the spring is unlocked so that it propels the astronaut upward. How high above that initial point does the astronaut rise?

The cable of the $1800\text{ kg}$ elevator cab in Fig. 8-45 snaps when the cab is at rest at the first floor, where the cab bottom is a distance $d = 3.7\text{ m}$ above a spring of spring constant $k = 0.15\text{ MN/m}$. A safety device clamps the cab against guide rails so that a constant frictional force of $4.4\text{ kN}$ opposes the cab’s motion. (a) Find the speed of the cab just before it hits the spring. (b) Find the maximum distance $x$ that the spring is compressed. (c) Find the distance that the cab will bounce back up the shaft. (d) Using conservation of energy, find the approximate total distance that the cab will move before coming to rest.

A particle can slide along a track with elevated ends and a flat central part, as shown in Fig. 8-47. The flat part has length $L = 40\text{ cm}$. The curved portions of the track are frictionless, but for the flat part the coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu_k = 0.20$. The particle is released from rest at point A, which is at height $h = L/2$. How far from the left edge of the flat part does the particle finally stop?

When accelerated along a straight line at $2.8 \times 10^{15}\text{ m/s}^2$ in a machine, an electron (mass $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$) has an initial speed of $1.4 \times 10^7\text{ m/s}$ and travels $5.8\text{ cm}$. Find (a) the final speed of the electron and (b) the increase in its kinetic energy.

On August 10, 1972, a large meteorite skipped across the atmosphere above the western United States and western Canada, much like a stone skipped across water. The meteorite’s mass was about $4 \times 10^6\text{ kg}$; its speed was about $15\text{ km/s}$. Had it entered the atmosphere vertically, it would have hit Earth’s surface with about the same speed. (a) Calculate the meteorite’s loss of kinetic energy (in joules) that would have been associated with the vertical impact. (b) Express the energy as a multiple of the explosive energy of 1 megaton of TNT, which is $4.2 \times 10^{15}\text{ J}$. (c) The energy associated with the atomic bomb explosion over Hiroshima was equivalent to 13 kilotons of TNT. To how many Hiroshima bombs would the meteorite impact have been equivalent?

A father racing his son has half the kinetic energy of the son, who has half the mass of the father. The father speeds up by $1.0\text{ m/s}$ and then has the same kinetic energy as the son. What are the original speeds of (a) the father and (b) the son?

A $3.0\text{ kg}$ body is at rest on a frictionless horizontal air track when a constant horizontal force $\vec{F}$ acting in the positive direction of an $x$ axis along the track is applied to the body. A stroboscopic graph of the position of the body as it slides to the right is shown in Fig. 7-18. The force is applied to the body at $t = 0$, and the graph records the position of the body at $0.50\text{ s}$ intervals. How much work is done on the body by the applied force between $t = 0$ and $t = 2.0\text{ s}$?

The only force acting on a $2.0\text{ kg}$ canister that is moving in an $xy$ plane has a magnitude of $5.0\text{ N}$. The canister initially has a velocity of $4.0\text{ m/s}$ in the positive $x$ direction and some time later has a velocity of $6.0\text{ m/s}$ in the positive $y$ direction. How much work is done on the canister by the $5.0\text{ N}$ force during this time?

A particle travels through a three-dimensional displacement given by $\vec{d} = (5.00\hat{i} - 3.00\hat{j} + 4.00\hat{k})\text{ m}$. If a force of magnitude $22.0\text{ N}$ and with fixed orientation does work on the particle, find the angle between the force and the displacement if the change in the particle’s kinetic energy is (a) $45.0\text{ J}$ and (b) $-45.0\text{ J}$.

A luge and its rider, with a total mass of $85\text{ kg}$, emerge from a downhill track onto a horizontal straight track with an initial speed of $37\text{ m/s}$. If a force slows them to a stop at a constant rate of $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$, (a) what magnitude $F$ is required for the force, (b) what distance $d$ do they travel while slowing, and (c) what work $W$ is done on them by the force? What are (d) $F$, (e) $d$, and (f) $W$ if they, instead, slow at $4.0\text{ m/s}^2$?
options: (a) $1.7 \times 10^2\text{ N}$; (b) $3.4 \times 10^2\text{ m}$; (c) $-5.8 \times 10^4\text{ J}$; (d) $3.4 \times 10^2\text{ N}$; (e) $1.7 \times 10^2\text{ m}$; (f) $-5.8 \times 10^4\text{ J}$
(a) $2.5 \times 10^2\text{ N}$; (b) $4.2 \times 10^2\text{ m}$; (c) $-3.5 \times 10^4\text{ J}$; (d) $5.0 \times 10^2\text{ N}$; (e) $2.1 \times 10^2\text{ m}$; (f) $-3.5 \times 10^4\text{ J}$

q: Figure 7-21 shows three forces applied to a trunk that moves leftward by $3.00\text{ m}$ over a frictionless floor. The force magnitudes are $F_1 = 5.00\text{ N}$, $F_2 = 9.00\text{ N}$, and $F_3 = 3.00\text{ N}$, and the indicated angle is $\theta = 60.0^\circ$. During the displacement, (a) what is the net work done on the trunk by the three forces and (b) does the kinetic energy of the trunk increase or decrease?

A military helicopter lifts a $75\text{ kg}$ flood survivor $16\text{ m}$ vertically from the river by a rope. If the acceleration of the survivor is $g/10$, how much work is done on the survivor by (a) the force from the helicopter and (b) the gravitational force on her? Just before she reaches the helicopter, what are her (c) kinetic energy and (d) speed?

In Fig. 7-23, a block of ice slides down a frictionless ramp at angle $50^\circ$ while an ice worker pulls on the block (via a rope) with a force that has a magnitude of $50\text{ N}$ and is directed up the ramp. As the block slides through distance $d = 0.50\text{ m}$ along the ramp, its kinetic energy increases by $80\text{ J}$. How much greater would its kinetic energy have been if the rope had not been attached to the block?

A cord is used to vertically lower an initially stationary block of mass $M$ at a constant downward acceleration of $g/4$. When the block has fallen a distance $d$, find (a) the work done by the cord’s force on the block, (b) the work done by the gravitational force on the block, (c) the kinetic energy of the block, and (d) the speed of the block.

In Fig. 7-25, a constant force $\vec{F}_a$ of magnitude $82.0\text{ N}$ is applied to a $3.00\text{ kg}$ shoe box at angle $\phi = 53.0^\circ$, causing the box to move up a frictionless ramp at constant speed. How much work is done on the box by $\vec{F}_a$ when the box has moved through vertical distance $h = 0.150\text{ m}$?

In Fig. 7-27, a $0.250\text{ kg}$ block of cheese lies on the floor of a $900\text{ kg}$ elevator cab that is being pulled upward by a cable through distance $d_1 = 2.40\text{ m}$ and then through distance $d_2 = 10.5\text{ m}$. (a) Through $d_1$, if the normal force on the block from the floor has constant magnitude $F_N = 3.00\text{ N}$, how much work is done on the cab by the force from the cable? (b) Through $d_2$, if the work done on the cab by the (constant) force from the cable is $92.61\text{ kJ}$, what is the magnitude of $F_N$?

A spring and block are in the arrangement of Fig. 7-10. When the block is pulled out to $x = +4.0\text{ cm}$, we must apply a force of magnitude $360\text{ N}$ to hold it there. We pull the block to $x = 11\text{ cm}$ and then release it. How much work does the spring do on the block as the block moves from $x_i = +5.0\text{ cm}$ to (a) $x = +3.0\text{ cm}$, (b) $x = -3.0\text{ cm}$, (c) $x = -5.0\text{ cm}$, and (d) $x = -9.0\text{ cm}$?

In the arrangement of Fig. 7-10, we gradually pull the block from $x = 0$ to $x = +3.0\text{ cm}$, where it is stationary. Figure 7-28 gives the work that our force does on the block. The scale of the figure’s vertical axis is set by $W_s = 1.0\text{ J}$. We then pull the block out to $x = +5.0\text{ cm}$ and release it from rest. How much work does the spring do on the block when the block moves from $x_i = +5.0\text{ cm}$ to (a) $x = +4.0\text{ cm}$, (b) $x = -2.0\text{ cm}$, and (c) $x = -5.0\text{ cm}$?

As a $2.5\text{ kg}$ body moves in the positive direction along an $x$ axis, a single force acts on it. The force is given by $F_x = 6x\text{ N}$, with $x$ in meters. The velocity at $x = 3.5\text{ m}$ is $8.5\text{ m/s}$. (a) Find the velocity of the body at $x = 4.5\text{ m}$. (b) Find the positive value of $x$ at which the body has a velocity of $5.5\text{ m/s}$.

The block in Fig. 7-10a lies on a horizontal frictionless surface, and the spring constant is $50\text{ N/m}$. Initially, the spring is at its relaxed length and the block is stationary at position $x = 0$. Then an applied force with a constant magnitude of $3.0\text{ N}$ pulls the block in the positive direction of the $x$ axis, stretching the spring until the block stops. When that stopping point is reached, what are (a) the position of the block, (b) the work that has been done on the block by the applied force, and (c) the work that has been done on the block by the spring force? During the block’s displacement, what are (d) the block’s position when its kinetic energy is maximum and (e) the value of that maximum kinetic energy?

The force on a particle is directed along an $x$ axis and given by $F = F_0(x/x_0 - 1)$. Find the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x = 0$ to $x = 2x_0$ by (a) plotting $F(x)$ and measuring the work from the graph and (b) integrating $F(x)$.

Figure 7-33 gives the acceleration of a $2.00\text{ kg}$ particle as an applied force moves it from rest along an $x$ axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 9.0\text{ m}$. The scale of the figure’s vertical axis is set by $a_s = 6.0\text{ m/s}^2$. How much work has the force done on the particle when the particle reaches (a) $x = 4.0\text{ m}$, (b) $x = 7.0\text{ m}$, and (c) $x = 9.0\text{ m}$? What is the particle’s speed and direction of travel when it reaches (d) $x = 4.0\text{ m}$, (e) $x = 7.0\text{ m}$, and (f) $x = 9.0\text{ m}$?
options: (a) $42\text{ J}$; (b) $30\text{ J}$; (c) $12\text{ J}$; (d) $6.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $5.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $3.5\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $50\text{ J}$; (b) $35\text{ J}$; (c) $18\text{ J}$; (d) $7.1\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $6.0\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $4.2\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $36\text{ J}$; (b) $24\text{ J}$; (c) $8\text{ J}$; (d) $5.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (e) $4.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis; (f) $2.8\text{ m/s}$, $+x$ axis
(a) $42\text{ J}$; (b) $30\text{ J}$; (c) $12\text{ J}$; (d) $6.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis; (e) $5.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis; (f) $3.5\text{ m/s}$, $-x$ axis

q: A particle of mass $0.020\text{ kg}$ moves along a curve with velocity $\vec{v}_1 = (5.0\hat{i} + 18\hat{k})\text{ m/s}$. After some time, the velocity changes to $\vec{v}_2 = (9.0\hat{i} + 22\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ due to the action of a single force. Find the work done on the particle during this interval of time.

Only one force is acting on a $2.8\text{ kg}$ particle-like object whose position is given by $x = 4.0t - 5.0t^2 + 2.0t^3$, with $x$ in meters and $t$ in seconds. What is the work done by the force from $t = 0\text{ s}$ to $t = 6.0\text{ s}$?

A force of $5.0\text{ N}$ acts on a $15\text{ kg}$ body initially at rest. Compute the work done by the force in (a) the first, (b) the second, and (c) the third seconds and (d) the instantaneous power due to the force at the end of the third second.

Across a horizontal floor, a $102\text{ kg}$ block is pulled at a constant speed of $5.5\text{ m/s}$ by an applied force of $125\text{ N}$ directed $38^\circ$ above the horizontal. Calculate the rate at which the force does work on the block.

A machine carries a $4.0\text{ kg}$ package from an initial position of $\vec{d}_i = (0.50\hat{i} + 0.75\hat{j} + 0.20\hat{k})\text{ m}$ at $t = 0$ to a final position of $\vec{d}_f = (7.50\hat{i} + 12.0\hat{j} + 7.20\hat{k})\text{ m}$ at $t = 12\text{ s}$. The constant force applied by the machine on the package is $\vec{F} = (2.00\hat{i} + 4.00\hat{j} + 6.00\hat{k})\text{ N}$. For that displacement, find (a) the work done on the package by the machine’s force and (b) the average power of the machine’s force on the package.

A fully loaded, slow-moving freight elevator has a cab with a total mass of $1200\text{ kg}$, which is required to travel upward $54\text{ m}$ in $3.0\text{ min}$, starting and ending at rest. The elevator’s counterweight has a mass of only $950\text{ kg}$, and so the elevator motor must help. What average power is required of the force the motor exerts on the cab via the cable?

A force $\vec{F} = (3.00\hat{i} + 7.00\hat{j} + 7.00\hat{k})\text{ N}$ acts on a $2.00\text{ kg}$ mobile object that moves from an initial position of $\vec{d}_i = (3.00\hat{i} - 2.00\hat{j} + 5.00\hat{k})\text{ m}$ to a final position of $\vec{d}_f = (-5.00\hat{i} + 4.00\hat{j} + 7.00\hat{k})\text{ m}$ in $4.00\text{ s}$. Find (a) the work done on the object by the force in the $4.00\text{ s}$ interval, (b) the average power due to the force during that interval, and (c) the angle between vectors $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{d}_f - \vec{d}_i$.

Adam stretches a spring by some length. John stretches the same spring later by three times the length stretched by Adam. Find the ratio of the stored energy in the first stretch to that in the second stretch.

You drop a $2.00\text{ kg}$ book to a friend who stands on the ground at distance $D = 10.0\text{ m}$ below. Your friend’s outstretched hands are at distance $d = 1.50\text{ m}$ above the ground (Fig. 8-19). (a) How much work $W_g$ does the gravitational force do on the book as it drops to her hands? (b) What is the change $\Delta U$ in the gravitational potential energy of the book–Earth system during the drop? If the gravitational potential energy $U$ of that system is taken to be zero at ground level, what is $U$ (c) when the book is released, and (d) when it reaches her hands? Now take $U$ to be $100\text{ J}$ at ground level and again find (e) $W_g$, (f) $\Delta U$, (g) $U$ at the release point, and (h) $U$ at her hands.

In Fig. 8-21, a $2.00\text{ g}$ ice flake is released from the edge of a hemispherical bowl whose radius $r$ is $22.0\text{ cm}$. The flake–bowl contact is frictionless. (a) How much work is done on the flake by the gravitational force during the flake’s descent to the bottom of the bowl? (b) What is the change in the potential energy of the flake–Earth system during that descent? (c) If that potential energy is taken to be zero at the bottom of the bowl, what is its value when the flake is released? (d) If, instead, the potential energy is taken to be zero at the release point, what is its value when the flake reaches the bottom of the bowl? (e) If the mass of the flake were doubled, would the magnitudes of the answers to (a) through (d) increase, decrease, or remain the same?
options: (a) $4.31\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-4.31\text{ mJ}$; (c) $4.31\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-4.31\text{ mJ}$; (e) all increase
(a) $2.15\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-2.15\text{ mJ}$; (c) $2.15\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-2.15\text{ mJ}$; (e) all decrease
(a) $8.62\text{ mJ}$; (b) $-8.62\text{ mJ}$; (c) $8.62\text{ mJ}$; (d) $-8.62\text{ mJ}$; (e) remain the same

q: Figure 8-23 shows a thin rod, of length $L = 2.00\text{ m}$ and negligible mass, that can pivot about one end to rotate in a vertical circle. A ball of mass $m = 5.00\text{ kg}$ is attached to the other end. The rod is pulled aside to angle $\theta_0 = 30.0^\circ$ and released with initial velocity $\vec{v}_0 = 0$. As the ball descends to its lowest point, (a) how much work does the gravitational force do on it and (b) what is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the ball–Earth system? (c) If the gravitational potential energy is taken to be zero at the lowest point, what is its value just as the ball is released? (d) Do the magnitudes of the answers to (a) through (c) increase, decrease, or remain the same if angle $\theta_0$ is increased?
options: (a) $9.8\text{ J}$; (b) $-9.8\text{ J}$; (c) $9.8\text{ J}$; (d) remain the same

q: In Problem 2, what is the speed of the car at (a) point A, (b) point B, and (c) point C? (d) How high will the car go on the last hill, which is too high for it to cross? (e) If we substituted a second car with twice the mass, what then are the answers to parts (a) through (d)?

q: (a) In Problem 5, what is the speed of the flake when it reaches the bottom of the bowl? (b) If we substituted a second flake with twice the mass, what would its speed be? (c) If, instead, we gave the flake an initial downward speed along the bowl, would the answer to part (a) increase, decrease, or remain the same?

A $5.0\text{ g}$ marble is fired vertically upward using a spring gun. The spring must be compressed $8.0\text{ cm}$ if the marble is to just reach a target $20\text{ m}$ above the marble’s position on the compressed spring. (a) What is the change $\Delta U_g$ in the gravitational potential energy of the marble–Earth system during the $20\text{ m}$ ascent? (b) What is the change $\Delta U_s$ in the elastic potential energy of the spring during its launch of the marble? (c) What is the spring constant of the spring?

In Fig. 8-24, a runaway truck with failed brakes is moving downgrade at $130\text{ km/h}$ just before the driver steers the truck up a frictionless emergency escape ramp with an inclination of $\theta = 15^\circ$. The truck’s mass is $1.2 \times 10^4\text{ kg}$. (a) What minimum length $L$ must the ramp have if the truck is to stop (momentarily) along it? (b) Does the minimum length $L$ increase, decrease, or remain the same if the truck’s mass is decreased and (c) its speed is decreased?

In Problem 6, what are the magnitudes of (a) the horizontal component and (b) the vertical component of the net force acting on the block at point Q? (c) At what height $h$ should the block be released from rest so that it is on the verge of losing contact with the track at the top of the loop? (d) Graph the magnitude of the normal force on the block at the top of the loop versus initial height $h$, for the range $h = 0$ to $h = 6R$.

A $1.0\text{ kg}$ block moving at $8.0\text{ m/s}$ strikes a spring fixed at one end to a wall and compresses the spring by $0.40\text{ m}$, where its speed gets reduced to $2.0\text{ m/s}$. After this event, the spring is mounted upright by fixing its bottom end to a floor, and a stone of mass $2.0\text{ kg}$ is placed on it; the spring is now compressed by $0.50\text{ m}$ from its rest length. The system is then released. How far above the rest-length point does the stone rise?

Figure 8-23 shows a pendulum of length $L = 1.25\text{ m}$. Its bob (which effectively has all the mass) has speed $v_0$ when the cord makes an angle $\theta_0 = 40.0^\circ$ with the vertical. (a) What is the speed of the bob when it is in its lowest position if $v_0 = 8.00\text{ m/s}$? What is the least value that $v_0$ can have if the pendulum is to swing down and then up (b) to a horizontal position, and (c) to a vertical position with the cord remaining straight? (d) Do the answers to parts (b) and (c) increase, decrease, or remain the same if $\theta_0$ is increased by a few degrees?
options: (a) $9.50\text{ m/s}$; (b) $5.50\text{ m/s}$; (c) $8.80\text{ m/s}$; (d) remain the same

q: The string in Fig. 8-26 is $L = 120\text{ cm}$ long, has a ball attached to one end, and is fixed at its other end. The distance $d$ from the fixed end to a fixed peg at point P is $75.0\text{ cm}$. When the initially stationary ball is released with the string horizontal as shown, it will swing along the dashed arc. What is its speed when it reaches (a) its lowest point and (b) its highest point after the string catches on the peg?

At $t = 0$ a $1.0\text{ kg}$ ball is thrown from a tall tower with $\vec{v}_0 = (18\text{ m/s})\hat{i} + (24\text{ m/s})\hat{j}$. What is $\Delta U$ of the ball–Earth system between $t = 0$ and $t = 6.0\text{ s}$ (still free fall)?

Tarzan, who weighs $688\text{ N}$, swings from a cliff at the end of a vine $18\text{ m}$ long (Fig. 8-28). From the top of the cliff to the bottom of the swing, he descends by $3.2\text{ m}$. The vine will break if the force on it exceeds $950\text{ N}$. (a) Does the vine break? (b) If it does not, what is the greatest force on it during the swing? If it does, at what angle with the vertical does it break?

A $4.00\text{ kg}$ block moves on a horizontal, frictionless surface and collides with a spring of spring constant $k$ that is fixed to a wall. When the block momentarily stops, the spring has been compressed by $0.20\text{ m}$. After rebounding, the block has a speed of $4.00\text{ m/s}$. Next, the spring is put on an inclined surface with its lower end fixed in place (Fig. 8-30). The same block is now released on the incline at a distance of $5.00\text{ m}$ from the spring’s free end. When the block momentarily stops, the spring has been compressed by $0.30\text{ m}$. (a) What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline? (b) How far does the block then move up the incline from the stopping point?

As shown in Fig. 8-32, the right end of a spring is fixed to a wall. A $1.00\text{ kg}$ block is then pushed against the free end so that the spring is compressed by $0.25\text{ m}$. After the block is released, it slides along a horizontal floor and (after leaving the spring) up an incline; both floor and incline are frictionless. Its maximum (vertical) height on the incline is $5.00\text{ m}$. What are (a) the spring constant and (b) the maximum speed? (c) If the angle of the incline is increased, what happens to the maximum (vertical) height?

In Fig. 8-34, a spring with $k = 170\text{ N/m}$ is at the top of a frictionless incline of angle $37.0^\circ$. The lower end of the incline is distance $D = 1.00\text{ m}$ from the end of the spring, which is at its relaxed length. A $2.00\text{ kg}$ canister is pushed against the spring until the spring is compressed $0.200\text{ m}$ and released from rest. (a) What is the speed of the canister at the instant the spring returns to its relaxed length (which is when the canister loses contact with the spring)? (b) What is the speed of the canister when it reaches the lower end of the incline?

In Fig. 8-30, a block of mass $m = 3.20\text{ kg}$ slides from rest a distance $d$ down a frictionless incline at angle $\theta = 30.0^\circ$ where it runs into a spring of spring constant $431\text{ N/m}$. When the block momentarily stops, it has compressed the spring by $21.0\text{ cm}$. What are (a) distance $d$ and (b) the distance between the point of the first block–spring contact and the point where the block’s speed is greatest?

At a lunar base, a uniform chain hangs over the edge of a horizontal platform. A machine does $1.0\text{ J}$ of work in pulling the rest of the chain onto the platform. The chain has a mass of $2.0\text{ kg}$ and a length of $3.0\text{ m}$. What length was initially hanging over the edge? On the Moon, the gravitational acceleration is $1/6$ of $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

The particle is released at $x = 4.5\text{ m}$ with an initial speed of $7.0\text{ m/s}$, headed in the negative $x$ direction. q: A single conservative force $F(x)$ acts on a $1.0\text{ kg}$ particle that moves along an $x$ axis. The potential energy $U(x)$ associated with $F(x)$ is given by $U(x) = -4x e^{-x/4}\text{ J}$, where $x$ is in meters. At $x = 5.0\text{ m}$ the particle has a kinetic energy of $2.0\text{ J}$. (a) What is the mechanical energy of the system?

In Fig. 8-39, a $3.5\text{ kg}$ block is accelerated from rest by a compressed spring of spring constant $640\text{ N/m}$. The block leaves the spring at the spring’s relaxed length and then travels over a horizontal floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.25$. The frictional force stops the block in distance $D = 7.8\text{ m}$. What are (a) the increase in the thermal energy of the block–floor system, (b) the maximum kinetic energy of the block, and (c) the original compression distance of the spring?

A loaded truck of mass $3000\text{ kg}$ moves on a level road at a constant speed of $6.000\text{ m/s}$. The frictional force on the truck from the road is $1000\text{ N}$. Assume that air drag is negligible. (a) How much work is done by the truck engine in $10.00\text{ min}$? (b) After $10.00\text{ min}$, the truck enters a hilly region whose inclination is $30^\circ$ and continues to move with the same speed for another $10.00\text{ min}$. What is the total work done by the engine during that period against the gravitational force and the frictional force? (c) What is the total work done by the engine in the full $20\text{ min}$?

A small block of mass $1/4\text{ kg}$ has an initial kinetic energy of $500\text{ J}$ while moving over the frictionless surface shown in Fig. 8-40. (a) Find the kinetic energy of block at Q. (b) If we assume that the potential energy at P is equal to zero, what is the potential energy of the block at R? (c) Find the speed of the block at R. (d) Find the change in the potential energy as the block moves from Q to R.

In Fig. 8-42, a $50\text{ kg}$ child rides a $2.0\text{ kg}$ seat down a frictionless slope from a height of $7.0\text{ m}$. Upon reaching the floor, the child and seat slide along it. There the coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.30$. How far along the floor do they slide?

In Fig. 8-43, a block of mass $m$ slides down three slides, each from a height $H$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is the same value $\mu$ for the slides. In terms of $m, H, \mu$, and $g$, what is the final kinetic energy of the block as it emerges from (a) slide a, (b) slide b, and (c) slide c?
A swimmer moves through the water at an average speed of $0.22\text{ m/s}$. The average drag force is $110\text{ N}$. What average power is required of the swimmer?

The total mechanical energy of a $2.00\text{ kg}$ particle moving along an $x$ axis is $5.00\text{ J}$. The potential energy is given as $U(x) = (x^4 - 2.00x^2)\text{ J}$, with $x$ in meters. Find the maximum velocity.

A block of mass $6.0\text{ kg}$ is pushed up an incline to its top by a man and then allowed to slide down to the bottom. The length of incline is $10\text{ m}$ and its height is $5.0\text{ m}$. The coefficient of friction between block and incline is $0.40$. Calculate (a) the work done by the gravitational force over the complete round trip of the block, (b) the work done by the man during the upward journey, (c) the mechanical energy loss due to friction over the round trip, and (d) the speed of the block when it reaches the bottom.

A stone with a weight of $5.29\text{ N}$ is launched vertically from ground level with an initial speed of $20.0\text{ m/s}$, and the air drag on it is $0.265\text{ N}$ throughout the flight. What are (a) the maximum height reached by the stone and (b) its speed just before it hits the ground?

A $10.0\text{ kg}$ block falls $30.0\text{ m}$ onto a vertical spring whose lower end is fixed to a platform. When the spring reaches its maximum compression of $0.200\text{ m}$, it is locked in place. The block is then removed and the spring apparatus is transported to the Moon, where the gravitational acceleration is $g/6$. A $50.0\text{ kg}$ astronaut then sits on top of the spring and the spring is unlocked so that it propels the astronaut upward. How high above that initial point does the astronaut rise?

The cable of the $1800\text{ kg}$ elevator cab in Fig. 8-45 snaps when the cab is at rest at the first floor, where the cab bottom is a distance $d = 3.7\text{ m}$ above a spring of spring constant $k = 0.15\text{ MN/m}$. A safety device clamps the cab against guide rails so that a constant frictional force of $4.4\text{ kN}$ opposes the cab’s motion. (a) Find the speed of the cab just before it hits the spring. (b) Find the maximum distance $x$ that the spring is compressed. (c) Find the distance that the cab will bounce back up the shaft. (d) Using conservation of energy, find the approximate total distance that the cab will move before coming to rest.

A particle can slide along a track with elevated ends and a flat central part, as shown in Fig. 8-47. The flat part has length $L = 40\text{ cm}$. The curved portions of the track are frictionless, but for the flat part the coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu_k = 0.20$. The particle is released from rest at point A, which is at height $h = L/2$. How far from the left edge of the flat part does the particle finally stop?

Three particles of mass $1.0\text{ kg}$, $2.0\text{ kg}$, and $3.0\text{ kg}$ are placed at the vertices A, B, and C, respectively, of an equilateral triangle ABC of edge $1.0\text{ m}$ (Fig. 9-23). Find the distance of their center of mass from A.

Figure 9-25 shows a slab with dimensions $d_1 = 11.0\text{ cm}$, $d_2 = 2.80\text{ cm}$, and $d_3 = 13.0\text{ cm}$. Half the slab consists of aluminum (density $= 2.70\text{ g/cm}^3$) and half consists of iron (density $= 7.85\text{ g/cm}^3$). What are (a) the $x$ coordinate, (b) the $y$ coordinate, and (c) the $z$ coordinate of the slab’s center of mass?
What are (a) the $x$ coordinate and (b) the $y$ coordinate of the center of mass for the uniform plate shown in Fig. 9-27 if $L = 5.0\text{ cm}$?

In the ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) molecule of Fig. 9-29, three hydrogen ($\text{H}$) atoms form an equilateral triangle, with the center of the triangle at distance $d = 9.40 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}$ from each hydrogen atom. The nitrogen ($\text{N}$) atom is at the apex of a pyramid, with the three hydrogen atoms forming the base. The nitrogen-to-hydrogen atomic mass ratio is $13.9$, and the nitrogen-to-hydrogen distance is $L = 10.14 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}$. What are the (a) $x$ and (b) $y$ coordinates of the molecule’s center of mass?

In the arrangement shown in Fig. 9-31, $m_A = 2.0\text{ kg}$ and $m_B = 1.0\text{ kg}$. The pulley is massless; the string is massless and long. The system is released at $t = 0\text{ s}$. Find (a) the acceleration of the center of mass of the blocks, (b) the displacement of the center of mass at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$, and (c) the speed of the center of mass when $m_A$ strikes the floor.

A big olive ($m = 0.50\text{ kg}$) lies at the origin of an $xy$ coordinate system, and a big Brazil nut ($M = 1.5\text{ kg}$) lies at the point $(1.0, 2.0)\text{ m}$. At $t = 0$, a force $\vec{F}_o = (2.0\hat{i} + 3.0\hat{j})\text{ N}$ begins to act on the olive, and a force $\vec{F}_n = (-3.0\hat{i} - 2.0\hat{j})\text{ N}$ begins to act on the nut. In unit-vector notation, what is the displacement of the center of mass of the olive–nut system at $t = 4.0\text{ s}$, with respect to its position at $t = 0$?

A shell is shot with an initial velocity of $20\text{ m/s}$, at an angle of $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$ with the horizontal. At the top of the trajectory, the shell explodes into two fragments of equal mass (Fig. 9-32). One fragment, whose speed immediately after the explosion is zero, falls vertically. How far from the gun does the other fragment land, assuming that the terrain is level and that air drag is negligible?

Figure 9-34 shows an arrangement with an air track, in which a cart is connected by a cord to a hanging block. The cart has mass $m_1 = 0.600\text{ kg}$, and its center is initially at $xy$ coordinates ($-0.500\text{ m}, 0\text{ m}$); the block has mass $m_2 = 0.400\text{ kg}$, and its center is initially at $xy$ coordinates ($0, -0.100\text{ m}$). The mass of the cord and pulley are negligible. The cart is released from rest, and both cart and block move until the cart hits the pulley. The friction between the cart and the air track and between the pulley and its axle is negligible. (a) In unit-vector notation, what is the acceleration of the center of mass of the cart–block system? (b) What is the velocity of the com as a function of time $t$? (d) If the path is straight, find the angle between it and the $x$ axis.

q: In Fig. 9-35a, a $4.5\text{ kg}$ dog stands on an $18\text{ kg}$ flatboat at distance $D = 6.1\text{ m}$ from the shore. It walks $2.4\text{ m}$ along the boat toward shore and then stops. Assuming no friction between the boat and the water, find how far the dog is then from the shore.

A $100\text{ kg}$ motorbike moves along AB at $10.0\text{ km/h}$, and after some time, the motorbike turns to travel along BC at the same speed as shown in Fig. 9-36. Find (a) the change in its kinetic energy and the (b) magnitude and (c) direction (relative to $+x$) of the change in its momentum.

A ball of mass $50\text{ g}$ moving with a speed of $2.0\text{ m/s}$ strikes a wall at an angle of incidence $45^\circ$ and is reflected from the wall at the same angle and with the same speed. See the overhead view in Fig. 9-38. Calculate (a) the magnitude of the change in the momentum of the ball, (b) the change in the magnitude of the momentum of the ball, and (c) the change in the magnitude of the momentum of the wall.

Until his seventies, Henri LaMothe (Fig. 9-40) excited audiences by belly-flopping from a height of $12\text{ m}$ into $30\text{ cm}$ of water. Assuming that he stops just as he reaches the bottom of the water and estimating his mass, find the magnitude of the impulse on him from the water.

A $5.00\text{ g}$ bullet moving at $100\text{ m/s}$ strikes a log. Assume that the bullet undergoes a uniform deceleration and stops after penetrating $6.00\text{ cm}$. Find (a) the time taken by the bullet to stop, (b) the impulse on the log, and (c) the magnitude of the average force experienced by the log.

A $3.00\text{ kg}$ block slides on a frictionless horizontal surface, first moving to the left at $50.0\text{ m/s}$. It collides with a spring whose other end is fixed to a wall, compresses the spring, and is brought to rest momentarily. Then it continues to be accelerated toward the right by the force of the compressed spring. The block acquires a final speed of $40.0\text{ m/s}$. It is in contact with the spring for $0.020\text{ s}$. Find (a) the magnitude and (b) the direction of the impulse of the spring force on the block. (c) What is the magnitude of the spring’s average force on the block?

A ball of mass $1.00\text{ kg}$ is attached to a loose string fixed to a ceiling. The ball is released from rest and falls $2.00\text{ m}$, where the string suddenly stops it. Find the impulse on it from the string.

Jumping up before the elevator hits. After the cable snaps and the safety system fails, an elevator cab free-falls from a height of $36\text{ m}$. During the collision at the bottom of the elevator shaft, a $90\text{ kg}$ passenger is stopped in $5.0\text{ ms}$. (Assume that neither the passenger nor the cab rebounds.) What are the magnitudes of the (a) impulse and (b) average force on the passenger during the collision? If the passenger were to jump upward with a speed of $7.0\text{ m/s}$ relative to the cab floor just before the cab hits the bottom of the shaft, what are the magnitudes of the (c) impulse and (d) average force?

Figure 9-43 shows a $0.300\text{ kg}$ baseball just before and just after it collides with a bat. Just before, the ball has velocity $\vec{v}_1$ of magnitude $12.0\text{ m/s}$ and angle $\theta_1 = 35.0^\circ$. Just after, it is traveling directly upward with velocity of magnitude $10.0\text{ m/s}$. The duration of the collision is $2.00\text{ ms}$. What are the (a) magnitude and (b) direction (relative to the positive direction of the $x$ axis) of the impulse on the ball from the bat? What are the (c) magnitude and (d) direction of the average force on the ball from the bat?

Figure 9-45 shows an approximate plot of force magnitude $F$ versus time $t$ during the collision of a $58\text{ g}$ Superball with a wall. The initial velocity of the ball is $34\text{ m/s}$ perpendicular to the wall; the ball rebounds directly back with approximately the same speed, also perpendicular to the wall. What is $F_{\text{max}}$, the maximum magnitude of the force on the ball from the wall during the collision?

A particle of unknown mass is acted upon by a force $\vec{F} = (100 e^{-2t}\hat{i})\text{ N}$. If at $t = 0.00\text{ s}$ the particle is at rest, for the time interval $t = 0.00\text{ s}$ to $t = 2.00\text{ s}$ find (a) the impulse on the particle and (b) the average force on the particle.

A man of mass $m_1 = 80\text{ kg}$ is standing on a platform of mass $m_2 = 20\text{ kg}$ that lies on a frictionless horizontal surface. The man starts moving on the platform with a velocity $v_r = 10\text{ m/s}$ relative to the platform. Find the recoil speed of the platform.

Figure 9-47 shows a two-ended “rocket” that is initially stationary on a frictionless floor, with its center at the origin of an $x$ axis. The rocket consists of a central block C (of mass $M = 6.00\text{ kg}$) and blocks L and R (each of mass $m = 2.00\text{ kg}$) on the left and right sides. Small explosions can shoot either of the side blocks away from block C and along the $x$ axis. Sequence: (1) At $t = 0$, block L is shot left with $3.00\text{ m/s}$ relative to C. (2) At $t = 0.80\text{ s}$, block R is shot right with $3.00\text{ m/s}$ relative to C. At $t = 2.80\text{ s}$, what are (a) the velocity of block C and (b) the position of its center?

In the Olympiad of 708 B.C., some athletes competing in the standing long jump used handheld weights called halteres to lengthen their jumps (Fig. 9-48). The weights were swung up in front just before liftoff and then swung down and thrown backward during the flight. Suppose a modern $78\text{ kg}$ long jumper similarly uses two $5.50\text{ kg}$ halteres, throwing them horizontally to the rear at his maximum height such that their horizontal velocity is zero relative to the ground. Let his liftoff velocity be $\vec{v} = (9.5\hat{i} + 4.0\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ with or without the halteres, and assume that he lands at the liftoff level. What distance would the use of the halteres add to his range?

A vase of mass $m$ falls onto a floor and breaks into three pieces that then slide across the frictionless floor. One piece of mass $0.25m$ moves at speed $v$ along an $x$ axis. The second piece of the same mass and speed moves along the $y$ axis. Find the speed of the third piece.

A particle of mass $2.0m$ is projected at an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal with a speed of $20\text{ m/s}$. After $1.0\text{ s}$, an explosion occurs and the particle is broken into two equal pieces. One piece is momentarily at rest before it falls. Find the maximum height attained by the other piece.

A bullet of mass $10\text{ g}$ strikes a ballistic pendulum of mass $2.0\text{ kg}$. The center of mass of the pendulum rises a vertical distance of $12\text{ cm}$. Assuming that the bullet remains embedded in the pendulum, calculate the bullet’s initial speed.

In Fig. 9-50a, a $3.50\text{ g}$ bullet is fired horizontally at two blocks at rest on a frictionless table. The bullet passes through block 1 (mass $1.20\text{ kg}$) and embeds itself in block 2 (mass $1.80\text{ kg}$). The blocks end up with speeds $v_1 = 0.630\text{ m/s}$ and $v_2 = 1.40\text{ m/s}$ (Fig. 9-50b). Neglecting the material removed from block 1 by the bullet, find the speed of the bullet as it (a) leaves and (b) enters block 1.

In Anchorage, collisions of a vehicle with a moose are so common that they are referred to with the abbreviation MVC. Suppose a $1000\text{ kg}$ car slides into a stationary $500\text{ kg}$ moose on a very slippery road, with the moose being thrown through the windshield. (a) What percentage of the original kinetic energy is lost in the collision to other forms of energy? (b) What percentage of the original kinetic energy is lost if the car hits a $300\text{ kg}$ camel? (c) Generally, does the percentage loss increase or decrease if the animal mass decreases?

Block 1 of mass $3.0\text{ kg}$ is sliding across a floor with speed $v_1 = 2.0\text{ m/s}$ when it makes a head-on, one-dimensional, elastic collision with initially stationary block 2 of mass $2.0\text{ kg}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the blocks and the floor is $\mu_k = 0.30$. Find the speeds of (a) block 1 and (b) block 2 just after the collision. Also find (c) their final separation after friction has stopped them and (d) the energy lost to thermal energy because of the friction.

In Fig. 9-53, a ball of mass $m = 60\text{ g}$ is shot with speed $v_i = 22\text{ m/s}$ into the barrel of a spring gun of mass $M = 240\text{ g}$ initially at rest on a frictionless surface. The ball sticks in the barrel at the point of maximum compression of the spring. Assume that the increase in thermal energy due to friction between the ball and the barrel is negligible. (a) What is the speed of the spring gun after the ball stops in the barrel? (b) What fraction of the initial kinetic energy of the ball is stored in the spring?

In Fig. 9-55, block 1 (mass $2.0\text{ kg}$) is moving rightward at $10\text{ m/s}$ and block 2 (mass $5.0\text{ kg}$) is moving rightward at $3.0\text{ m/s}$. The surface is frictionless, and a spring with a spring constant of $1120\text{ N/m}$ is fixed to block 2. When the blocks collide, the compression of the spring is maximum at the instant the blocks have the same velocity. Find the maximum compression.

Two bodies of masses $m = 0.30\text{ kg}$ and $2m$ are connected by a long string of negligible mass. The string is looped over a pulley and, with the string taut, the bodies are released at time $t = 0$ so that the heavier one descends and the lighter one ascends. At time $t = 4.0\text{ s}$, the lighter one undergoes a fully inelastic collision with a third body of mass $m$. Because the first two bodies move in rigid fashion, the collision is effectively between the third body and the system of the first two bodies. (a) Just after the collision, what is the speed of the three bodies? (b) By how much was the kinetic energy of the descending body decreased because of the collision?

Block 1 of mass $m_1$ slides along a frictionless floor and into a one-dimensional elastic collision with stationary block 2 of mass $m_2 = 3m_1$. Prior to the collision, the center of mass of the two-block system had a speed of $3.00\text{ m/s}$. Afterward, what are the speeds of (a) the center of mass and (b) block 2?

Particle 1 with mass $m$ and velocity $v\hat{i}$ and particle 2 with mass $2m$ and velocity $-2v\hat{i}$ are moving toward each other along an $x$ axis when they undergo a one-dimensional elastic collision. After the collision, what are the velocities of (a) particle 1 and (b) particle 2? What is the velocity of the center of mass of the two-particle system (c) before and (d) after the collision?

In Fig. 9-58, particle 1 of mass $m_1 = 0.30\text{ kg}$ slides rightward along an $x$ axis on a frictionless floor with a speed of $2.0\text{ m/s}$. When it reaches $x = 0$, it undergoes a one-dimensional elastic collision with stationary particle 2 of mass $m_2 = 0.40\text{ kg}$. When particle 2 then reaches a wall at $x_w = 70\text{ cm}$, it bounces from the wall with no loss of speed. At what position on the $x$ axis does particle 2 then collide with particle 1?

A small ball of mass $m$ is aligned above a larger ball of mass $M = 0.63\text{ kg}$ (with a slight separation, as with the baseball and basketball of Fig. 9-60a), and the two are dropped simultaneously from a height of $h = 1.8\text{ m}$. (Assume the radius of each ball is negligible relative to $h$.) (a) If the larger ball rebounds elastically from the floor and then the small ball rebounds elastically from the larger ball, what value of $m$ results in the larger ball stopping when it collides with the small ball? (b) What height does the small ball then reach (Fig. 9-60b)?

In Fig. 9-21, projectile particle 1 is an alpha particle and target particle 2 is an oxygen nucleus. The alpha particle is scattered at angle $\theta_1 = 64.0^\circ$ and the oxygen nucleus recoils with speed $1.20 \times 10^5\text{ m/s}$ and at angle $\theta_2 = 51.0^\circ$. In atomic mass units, the mass of the alpha particle is $4.00\text{ u}$ and the mass of the oxygen nucleus is $16.0\text{ u}$. What are the (a) final and (b) initial speeds of the alpha particle?

After a completely inelastic collision, two objects of the same mass and same initial speed move away together at half their initial speed. Find the angle between the initial velocities of the objects.

In Fig. 9-63, a bob of mass $10m$ is suspended from an inextensible string with negligible mass. When the bob is in equilibrium (at rest), two particles each of mass $m$ strike it simultaneously with the speeds indicated. The particles stick to the bob. Find (a) the magnitude of the net impulse on the string due to the collision, (b) the velocity of the system just after the collision, and (c) the mechanical energy lost in the collision.

In Fig. 9-64, two long barges are moving in the same direction in still water, one with a speed of $10\text{ km/h}$ and the other with a speed of $20\text{ km/h}$. While they are passing each other, coal is shoveled from the slower to the faster one at a rate of $1000\text{ kg/min}$. How much additional force must be provided by the driving engines of (a) the faster barge and (b) the slower barge if neither is to change speed? Assume that the shoveling is always perfectly sideways and that the frictional forces between the barges and the water do not depend on the mass of the barges.

A rocket that is set for a vertical launch has a mass of $50.0\text{ kg}$ and contains $450\text{ kg}$ of fuel. The rocket can have a maximum exhaust velocity of $2.00\text{ km/s}$. What should be the minimum rate of fuel consumption (a) to just lift it off the launching pad and (b) to give it an acceleration of $20.0\text{ m/s}^2$? (c) If the consumption rate is set at $10.0\text{ kg/s}$, what is the rocket speed at the moment when the fuel is fully consumed?
